title: Spend Some Time with Fairies
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the history and lore of fairies, starting with the point that fairies as understood today are a relatively recent concept while folklore across Europe goes back far earlier. They cover the links between elves and fairies, the Tuatha Dé Danann origin theory, fairy forts, the word "fairy" and its adjective sense, the medieval Church's demonization of fairies, nineteenth-century folklore collectors (the Grimms, Anna Eliza Bray, W.B. Yeats), the Victorian winged fairy and John Anster Fitzgerald, the 1917 Cottingley Fairies hoax and Arthur Conan Doyle's endorsement, Briggs's seven fairy categories (heroic trooping, homely trooping, solitary, tutelary/brownies, nature, and catch-all), fairy lore about iron, holy water, church bells and changelings, famous fairies like Puck, Queen Mab, Tinker Bell and the Tooth Fairy, and Disney fairies. The episode also includes a brief tangent on the film The Substance and a listener email from Brad correcting a Monopoly Mr. Monopoly monocle myth.

segments.title: Opening and what fairies are
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the episode on fairies and note that fairies as understood today are a relatively recent concept, with no single agreed definition.

segments.title: Elves, early fairy lore and origins
segments.summary: Early elf lore was associated with illness and misfortune; the word ælfwine-style 'elf friend' name is mentioned; Ronald Hutton's scholarship; theory linking fairies to the Tuatha Dé Danann.

segments.title: Irish fairy forts and the Irish fairy belief
segments.summary: Irish elves descended from an earlier magic-using people and lived on in fairy forts and mounds; a road in County Clare in 1999 was rerouted to avoid a fairy bush; fairy belief revived as Irish nationalist pride.

segments.title: Classical roots and the word fairy
segments.summary: Classical Greek and Roman stories influenced human-like fairies; the word 'fairy' came from the Latin fata and the adjective sense of magical or uncanny; 'stroke' is linked to 'elf stroke'.

segments.title: Medieval fairies, Merlin and duality
segments.summary: Medieval traditions of human-like fairies; fairies could be good or evil depending on how they were treated; Merlin and Morgan le Fay from Arthurian legend discussed.

segments.title: Church condemnation of fairies
segments.summary: In the thirteenth century the Church declared fairies absent from the Bible and therefore evil or devils, and people were told to stop associating with them.

segments.title: Nineteenth-century revival: Grimm, Bray and Yeats
segments.summary: Interest revived in the nineteenth century; the Brothers Grimm's tales; Anna Eliza Bray's 1844 collection from Devonshire where fairies were tied to unbaptized babies; W.B. Yeats's 1888 Irish fairy guide.

segments.title: Victorian winged fairies and John Anster Fitzgerald
segments.summary: Wings appeared in literature in the early eighteenth century; the Victorian era popularized winged, insect-like fairies; painter John Anster Fitzgerald's 'Rabbit and Fairies' is discussed.

segments.title: The fairy loophole in art
segments.summary: Artists used fairies as a workaround to paint nude figures under censorship, called the fairy loophole.

segments.title: Cottingley Fairies hoax (1917)
segments.summary: Elsie Wright and Francis Griffiths took photos of fairies near Cottingley, England, in 1917 using paper cutouts from a children's book held with hairpins; Elsie's mother took them to the Theosophical Society; Arthur Conan Doyle endorsed them; Francis admitted the hoax in 1983.

segments.title: Briggs's fairy categories
segments.summary: Katharine Briggs's 1957 categorization: heroic trooping, homely trooping, solitary (such as leprechauns and Tom Tit Tot), tutelary fairies including brownies, nature fairies, and a catch-all of giants and monsters.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break with banter about pudding skin.

segments.title: Tangent on The Substance
segments.summary: Chuck and Josh discuss the body horror film The Substance and the 1980s film Society.

segments.title: Fairy characteristics: dual nature, rules and iron
segments.summary: Fairies could be immortal or soulless; they cannot cross running water, dislike holy water, cold iron, church bells and mention of Sunday; they are called fair folk; magic ointment lore.

segments.title: Changelings and protection of babies
segments.summary: Folklore that fairies swapped human babies for changelings; families used Bibles, iron tongs or scissors for protection; some killed the suspected changeling, a grim practice in poor families.

segments.title: Famous fairies: Puck, Queen Mab and Shakespeare
segments.summary: Puck in A Midsummer Night's Dream as a mischievous fairy or demon; Shakespeare's Queen Mab possibly invented by him.

segments.title: Tinker Bell, fairy dust and the Tooth Fairy
segments.summary: J.M. Barrie created Tinker Bell and fairy dust in Peter Pan; the Tooth Fairy traces to Norse tooth fee tradition and a 1908 Chicago Tribune article.

segments.title: Disney fairies
segments.summary: Hosts list Disney fairies including Cinderella's fairy godmother, fairies in Fantasia, and Sleeping Beauty's Flora, Fauna and Merryweather.

segments.title: Children's fairy book recommendation
segments.summary: Chuck recalls a children's fairy book series, Backyard Fairies by Phoebe Wahl.

segments.title: Listener mail from Brad on Monopoly's monocle
segments.summary: Brad corrects the belief that Rich Uncle Pennybags wore a monocle, calling it a Mandela effect example.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts thank Brad and give the show's contact and credits.
